sections.title: Section 1: Diving into AI First Java Programming

chapters.title: Chapter 1: Your First Java Program
chapters.goal: Build a simple application using an IDE and AI tooling and learn the syntax of Java that makes your program run.

examples.title: Hello World
examples.description: Write a simple Hello World program in Java.
examples.prompt: Write a Hello World program in Java.

explanation.summary: This is the classic first Java program: it prints the greeting "Hello, World!" to the screen and then ends. It shows the minimum structure every Java program needs.

lines.text: All Java code lives inside a class, and this one is named HelloWorld. The file must be saved as HelloWorld.java so the name matches exactly.

This is the method Java looks for when it starts a program, so execution always begins here. The words public, static, void, and String[] args are required in this exact form for Java to recognise it as the starting point.

System.out is the standard output stream, the text console, and println writes the given text followed by a line break. The text in double quotes is a string literal, meaning the characters are printed exactly as written.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Dynamic Programming with Variables and Input
chapters.goal: Generate an application that you can interact with and learn how variables act as the memory of software programs.

examples.title: Variable Declaration
examples.description: Declare variables in Java to remember values for later.
examples.prompt: Create a reminder by declaring a String variable and print the reminder.
response: String reminder = "Don't forget to submit the report by 5 PM.";

explanation.summary: This program stores a reminder message in a String variable and then prints it to the screen. It shows the basic pattern of naming a piece of text so you can refer to it later.

lines.text: Every Java program lives inside a class, and the class name must match the file name, so this code belongs in DisplayReminder.java.
This is the method Java looks for when it starts a program; execution begins with the first line inside it.

lines.code: String reminder = "Don't forget to submit the report by 5 PM.";
lines.text: This declares a variable named reminder of type String, which holds text, and assigns the message to it. Text values must be wrapped in double quotes.
Passing the variable name rather than the quoted text prints whatever value the variable currently holds, so the message only has to be written once.

examples.title: Print Number
examples.description: Create a Java program that displays a number variable.

prompts.prompt: Write code that prints a number variable.

explanation.summary: This program stores the whole number 42 in a variable and prints it to the screen. It shows that println can display numbers, not just text in quotes.

lines.text: Every Java program lives inside a class, and the class name must match the file name, so this code belongs in PrintNumber.java.
This is the method Java runs first when the program starts; all the work happens inside its braces.
The keyword int declares a variable that holds whole numbers, and the value 42 is stored in it under the name number.
Passing the variable without quotation marks prints the value it holds; writing "number" instead would print the word itself.

prompts.prompt: Update the code to add two numbers and display their sum.

explanation.summary: This program stores two whole numbers in variables, adds them together into a third variable, and prints the result. It shows how a variable can hold the outcome of a calculation rather than a value you typed yourself.

lines.text: Every Java program lives inside a class, and the class name must match the file name, so this code belongs in PrintNumber.java.
This is the method Java runs first when the program starts; anything you want executed goes inside it.
Declares a variable named a of type int, which holds whole numbers, and stores 20 in it.
Declares a second int variable so the program has two values to work with.
The expression on the right is evaluated first, then the result 42 is stored in a new variable named sum. Naming the result makes the code easier to read and lets you reuse the value later.
Prints the value held in sum. Because there are no quotation marks, Java prints the number stored in the variable rather than the word "sum".

examples.title: Java Data Types: Short and Int
examples.description: Explore the differences between short and int data types in Java.
examples.prompt: Write intro code using both a short data type and an int data type.
response: int sum = shortValue + intValue;    // short promoted to int
short doubled = (short) (shortValue * 2); // cast back to short

explanation.summary: This program stores whole numbers in two different integer types, short and int, then shows what happens when you combine them in arithmetic. It demonstrates that Java automatically promotes a short to an int in a calculation, and that going the other direction requires an explicit cast.

lines.text: A short holds whole numbers in 16 bits, so its range is -32,768 to 32,767. The underscore in 12_345 is a readability aid for long digit strings and is ignored by the compiler.
An int uses 32 bits and is the usual choice for whole numbers in Java, comfortably holding values into the billions.

lines.code: int sum = shortValue + intValue;    // short promoted to int
lines.text: When a short and an int are added, Java widens the short to an int first, so the result is an int and fits in the sum variable without any extra work.

lines.code: short doubled = (short) (shortValue * 2); // cast back to short
lines.text: The multiplication produces an int, so (short) is required to narrow it back down. Here 24,690 still fits in a short, but a larger value would silently wrap around.
Using + with a String on the left converts the number to text and joins it, which is how these labelled values are built.

examples.title: Java Data Types: Widening Type Casting
examples.description: Explore widening type casting in Java by converting integer variables to double in a calculation.
examples.prompt: Write code to calculate splitting the length of a piece of printer paper into 2 pieces, converting two integer variables to a double in the calculation.
response: int paperLengthInches = 11; // length of printer paper (US Letter long side)

explanation.summary: This program divides the 11-inch length of a sheet of US Letter paper into two pieces and prints the length of each. Because both values are whole numbers, they are converted to double first so the division keeps its fractional part.

lines.code: int paperLengthInches = 11; // length of printer paper (US Letter long side)
lines.text: The long side of a US Letter sheet is a whole number of inches, so int is a natural fit for storing it.
The number of pieces to cut is also a count, which is why it is an int as well.
The (double) casts widen each integer into a decimal number before the division happens. Without them, Java would perform integer division and throw away any remainder.
Joining text and the double with + builds one message; Java converts the number to text automatically as it is concatenated.

examples.title: Java Data Types: Narrow Type Casting
examples.description: Explore narrowing type casting in Java by converting a double variable to an int.
examples.prompt: Write code to narrow casting by displaying an integer value of a price of $100.30 for an advertisement.
response: int adPrice = (int) price; // narrow casting from double to int

explanation.summary: This program stores a price with cents in a double, then converts it to an int so only the whole dollars remain. It shows narrowing casting: turning a larger type into a smaller one, which discards the fractional part.

lines.text: A double holds numbers with a decimal point, so it can store the full price of 100.30 including the cents.

lines.code: int adPrice = (int) price; // narrow casting from double to int
lines.text: The (int) in front of price is a cast that forces the double into an int. Java will not do this automatically because information is lost: the .30 is chopped off, not rounded, leaving 100.
Joining text to a number with + turns the number into text, so the output reads as a single sentence with the rounded-down dollar amount.

examples.title: Java Data Types: Float and Double
examples.description: Explore the differences between float and double data types in Java.
examples.prompt: Write intro code using both a float data type and a double data type.
response: double sum = f + d;              // float promoted to double
float narrowed = (float) d;      // explicit cast from double to float

explanation.summary: This program stores a decimal number in a float and a more precise decimal in a double, then shows what happens when the two are mixed in arithmetic and when a double is forced back into a float.

lines.text: A float holds about seven significant digits. The trailing f is required, because Java treats a plain decimal literal as a double and will not silently squeeze it into a float.
A double uses twice the memory and holds roughly fifteen significant digits, which is why it is the default choice for decimal numbers in Java.
Joining a number to a string with + converts the number to text so it can be printed.

lines.code: double sum = f + d;              // float promoted to double
lines.text: When a float and a double meet in the same expression, Java widens the float to a double first, so the result is a double and no precision is lost.

lines.code: float narrowed = (float) d;      // explicit cast from double to float
lines.text: Going from double to float discards precision, so Java demands the explicit (float) cast as proof that you accept the loss.
The printed value shows the truncated digits, making the cost of narrowing visible.

examples.title: Java Data Types: Boolean
examples.description: Explore the boolean data type in Java.
examples.prompt: Write intro code using a boolean data type without using logic like an if statement.
response: // Combine booleans with logical operators (no if/switch/?:)

explanation.summary: This program shows Java's boolean type, which holds only true or false. It creates booleans directly, produces them from number comparisons, and combines them with the logical operators AND (&&) and NOT (!) — all without any if statement.

lines.text: A boolean variable can hold exactly one of two values, and here it is set literally to true.
The other of the two possible boolean values; names starting with "is" or "has" read naturally as yes/no questions.
When a boolean is joined to a string with +, Java writes it out as the word true or false.
Two plain integers are set up so the comparisons below have real numbers to work with.
The == operator tests whether two values are equal and yields a boolean, so the result of 3 == 5 can be stored in a variable. Note that == compares, while a single = assigns.
Comparison operators such as > also produce booleans, so this holds true because 3 is greater than 0.
The ! operator flips a boolean to its opposite, and && is true only when both sides are true; together they say some tests passed but not all of them.
Several conditions chained with && demand that every one be true, and because allPassed is false the whole expression is false.

examples.title: Pizza Party Calculator
examples.description: Create a pizza calculator in Java that calculates the number of pizzas needed based on the number of people in a party and slices per pizza.
examples.prompt: Write a simple pizza calculator with variables for people in party and slices per pizza.

explanation.summary: This program works out how many pizzas a party needs. It stores the number of guests, slices per pizza, and slices per person in variables, then computes the total slices and rounds the pizza count up so nobody goes hungry.

lines.text: The guest count is stored in a variable rather than typed into the calculation, so a different party size only needs one edit here.
How many slices one pizza is cut into; this is the divisor used later to turn slices into whole pizzas.
The appetite assumption behind the estimate, kept separate so it can be raised or lowered on its own.
Multiplying guests by slices each gives the total demand in slices, which is easier to reason about than pizzas.

Integer division in Java throws away any remainder, so adding slicesPerPizza - 1 first forces a partly used pizza to count as a whole one. This is the standard trick for rounding up with whole numbers.
The plus sign joins text to a number here, and Java automatically converts the number into characters for printing.
With 10 people eating 2 slices each, 20 slices are needed, and the rounding up turns 2.5 pizzas into 3.

examples.title: Welcome {Name}
examples.description: Write a Welcome {Name} program in Java using a variable to store the name.
examples.prompt: Write a Welcome {Name} application without taking input.

explanation.summary: This program stores a name in a variable and prints a greeting that includes it. It is the version without user input, so the name is fixed in the code.

lines.text: A String variable holds a sequence of text characters, written between double quotes. Naming the value gives you one place to change it later.

The + operator joins two pieces of text into one, so the greeting and the stored name print as a single line. Note the space at the end of "Welcome " 
u2014 without it the output would read "WelcomeAda".

examples.title: Welcome {Name} with Input
examples.description: Write a simple Welcome {Name} program in Java that takes the user's name as input.
examples.prompt: Write a simple Welcome {Name} program in Java that accepts the user's name as input.

explanation.summary: This program asks the user to type their name, reads what they type, and greets them by name. It is the first program in the chapter that reacts to input instead of using a value fixed in the code.

lines.text: A Scanner is the tool Java uses to read what someone types. Here it is created with the fully qualified name java.util.Scanner because no import statement has been added yet, and System.in tells it to read from the keyboard.
Using print instead of println leaves the cursor on the same line, so the person types their answer right after the prompt.
nextLine reads everything the user types up to the Enter key and stores it in the String variable name, so full names with spaces are kept intact.
The plus sign joins the fixed text to the value held in name, producing a greeting that changes with every run.
Closing the Scanner releases the resource it was holding; it is good habit to close what you open once you are done reading.

examples.title: Calculate cake servings with division and modulus operators
examples.prompt: Create an intro Java example for serving 2 cake slices per person using mathematical operators for division and modulus.
response: int peopleFullyServed = slicesAvailable / slicesPerPerson; // integer division

explanation.summary: This program splits 23 cake slices into portions of 2 per person, then reports how many people get a full portion and how many slices are left over. It shows the difference between Java's division operator and its remainder operator.

lines.text: The total number of slices is stored as an int because slices are counted in whole units. The value 23 is deliberately odd so that the leftover calculation has something to show.
Naming the serving size in a variable makes the intent clear and lets you change the portion size in one place.

lines.code: int peopleFullyServed = slicesAvailable / slicesPerPerson; // integer division
lines.text: When both operands are ints, Java's / performs integer division and discards any fraction, so 23 / 2 gives 11 rather than 11.5. That is exactly what you want here, since a person served only half a portion is not fully served.
The % operator returns what is left after the division, so 23 % 2 gives 1. Division and modulus are a pair: together they account for every slice.
The + here joins text to a number, converting the int to its printed form so the label and the value appear as one line.
Printing the computed result alongside the inputs lets you verify the arithmetic at a glance.

examples.title: Import statement instead of full package name for Scanner
examples.prompt: Rewrite this code to use an import statement for Scanner rather than the full package within the code.

explanation.summary: This program asks for your name, reads what you type, and greets you. It uses an import statement at the top so the class can be referred to as just Scanner instead of java.util.Scanner.

lines.text: This tells the compiler where to find the Scanner class, so the rest of the file can write the short name Scanner instead of the full java.util.Scanner every time.
Creates a Scanner that reads from System.in, the keyboard input stream. Thanks to the import, the type name is short and the code reads more cleanly.
Uses print rather than println so the cursor stays on the same line, letting the reader type their answer right after the prompt.
Reads one whole line of typed input, including any spaces, and stores it in the variable name.
The + joins the fixed text and the value the user entered into a single greeting.
Releases the resources the Scanner was holding, which is good practice once you are finished reading input.

examples.title: Example showing boolean data type
examples.prompt: Write intro code using a boolean data type without conditional logic.

explanation.summary: This program stores two true/false values in boolean variables, prints them, and then combines them with logical operators to produce a third boolean. It shows that boolean values can be computed and displayed like any other data, without needing an if statement.

lines.text: A boolean variable holds only one of two values, true or false. Note that true is a Java keyword, not the text "true" in quotes.
The second boolean starts out false, which will matter when the two are combined below.
When a boolean is joined to a string with +, Java automatically converts it to the words true or false for display.
The && operator yields true only when both sides are true, and ! flips a boolean to its opposite. So this reads as "Java is fun and there are no bugs," which works out to true.
Printing the computed result shows that logical expressions produce a boolean value you can store and reuse, with no conditional statement involved.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Controlling Code with Conditions and Loops
chapters.goal: Learn how to apply control structures in order to build more advanced applications that make use of logic and iteration.

examples.title: If Statement
examples.description: Create a Java program that displays a game's level if a condition is met.

prompts.prompt: Write a Java program without input that prints 'Novice Level' if the number variable is less than 10.

explanation.summary: This program stores the number 5 in a variable and checks whether it is below 10. Because it is, the message "Novice Level" appears on screen; if the number were 10 or more, the program would print nothing at all.

lines.text: Declares a variable named number that holds whole numbers and gives it the starting value 5. Changing this value is how you test the other branch of the decision below.
The condition inside the parentheses is either true or false; the block that follows runs only when it is true. Here 5 < 10 is true, so the block runs.
The indentation and the surrounding braces show that this statement belongs to the if, so it is skipped entirely whenever the condition is false.

prompts.prompt: Update the code to add an else to print 'Expert Level' and update the variable to fit that criterion.

explanation.summary: This program checks a player's score against a threshold and prints one of two skill levels. It shows how an if/else pair picks exactly one of two paths depending on whether a condition is true or false.

lines.text: Stores the value the decision will be based on. Because 12 is not below 10, this value is chosen to make the else branch run.
Tests whether the value is less than 10. The block that follows runs only when this comparison is true.
The result for a low number, which is skipped here since 12 is not less than 10.
Provides the fallback path taken whenever the if condition is false, so one of the two messages always prints.
The message that actually appears when the program runs, because the condition failed.

prompts.prompt: Add an else if for an 'Intermediate Level'.

explanation.summary: This program picks a game level based on a player's score using a chain of conditions. Because the value 12 is not below 10 but is below 20, it prints "Intermediate Level".

lines.text: Stores the score to be tested. Changing this one value is how you exercise each of the three branches below.
The first condition is checked before any other. Since 12 is not less than 10, Java moves on to the next test.
An else if adds a second test that Java only reaches when the first condition was false, which is why this branch means "10 or more, but under 20".
This is the line that runs for this program, because 12 falls in the middle range.
The else is the catch-all: it runs only when every condition above it failed, covering scores of 20 and up.

examples.title: Ternary Operator
examples.description: Create a Java program that uses a ternary operator to print a game level.
examples.prompt: Use a ternary operator to print a game level as novice, intermediate, or expert based on a number variable.
response: int levelNumber = 17; // change this value to test

explanation.summary: This program picks a game level name from a number using the ternary operator, a compact one-line alternative to an if/else chain, and prints the result.

lines.code: int levelNumber = 17; // change this value to test
lines.text: The score being classified is stored in a variable so you can edit one number and rerun the program to see each branch.
The ternary operator evaluates the test before the question mark and produces the value after it when the test is true, so a number under 10 yields "novice".
The part after the colon is the value used when the first test fails, and here it is another ternary that checks the next threshold.
The final colon supplies the fallback value when neither test succeeded; a ternary must always produce a value, so this last branch cannot be omitted.
The whole chain resolved to a single String, which is now printed.

examples.title: Switch/Case Statement
examples.description: Create a Java program that displays the status of a process based on a number variable.
examples.prompt: Use a switch statement to evaluate a status number variable and print 'Starting' for 1, 'Processing' for 2, 'Ready' for 3, and 'Unknown' as default.

explanation.summary: This program stores an order status as a number and uses a switch statement to print the matching description. Because status is 2, it prints "Processing".

lines.text: The status is held as a plain integer code, which is exactly the kind of value a switch is designed to test.
A switch compares one value against several fixed alternatives, which is clearer than a long chain of if/else if tests.
Each case names one possible value of status; execution jumps to the matching label.
This is the body that runs when status is 1.
The break exits the switch. Without it, execution would fall through into the next case and print more than one message.
This is the label that matches here, since status was set to 2.
The default branch catches every value that no case listed, so unexpected status codes still produce sensible output.
The last branch needs no break because the switch ends right after it.

examples.title: While/Do-While Loop
examples.description: Create a Java program that uses while and do-while loops to print numbers.

prompts.prompt: Write a coffee order program using a while loop to print the status and increment until it reaches 100.

explanation.summary: This program tracks a coffee order's progress from 0% to 100%, printing the status at each step and announcing when the drink is ready. It uses a while loop, which keeps repeating as long as its condition stays true.

lines.text: The counter starts at zero because the order has made no progress yet. A while loop needs this variable to exist before the loop begins, since the loop's condition tests it.
Java checks this condition before each pass through the loop body. Using <= rather than < means 100 itself gets printed, so the reader sees the full range from 0% to 100%.
Joining text and a number with + turns the number into text, producing a line like "Coffee order status: 30%".
This is the step that eventually ends the loop. Forgetting to change the variable a while condition depends on is the classic cause of an infinite loop.
Sitting outside the loop's braces, this runs once after the condition finally fails and the loop is done.

prompts.prompt: Change the code to use a do-while loop instead of a while loop.

explanation.summary: This program counts a coffee order's progress from 0% to 100% in steps of 10, printing each status, then announces the order is ready. It uses a do-while loop, which runs its body once before ever checking the condition.

lines.text: The starting progress of the order; the loop will raise this value until it passes 100.
A do-while loop puts the body first, so the statements inside always run at least once even if the condition turns out to be false.
Reports the current progress; the + operator joins the number to the surrounding text to build one message.
Advances the progress by 10 on each pass. Without this the condition would never become false and the loop would run forever.
The condition is tested after each pass: as long as status has not gone past 100 the body repeats, so the loop prints 0% through 100%. Note the semicolon, which is required at the end of a do-while.
Runs once after the loop finishes, confirming that the counting has reached its end.

examples.title: For Loop
examples.description: Create a Java program that loops through numbers or items in a list and prints each one.

prompts.prompt: Use a for loop to increment a lap number variable and print each lap.

explanation.summary: This program uses a for loop to count laps from 1 to 3, printing each lap number, then prints a final message once the loop finishes.

lines.text: A for loop gathers all three parts of counting into one line: it creates lap starting at 1, keeps going while lap is 3 or less, and adds 1 to lap after each pass.
Joining text to a number with + produces a single string, so each pass reports the current value of lap.
This line sits outside the loop body, so it runs once after the counting has finished.

prompts.prompt: Update the for loop to decrement the lap instead.

explanation.summary: This program counts down from lap 3 to lap 1 using a for loop, then prints a closing message. It shows that a for loop can run backwards by decrementing its counter.

lines.text: The three parts of a for loop are the start value, the condition to keep going, and the step. Starting at 3, continuing while lap is at least 1, and using lap-- to subtract one each pass makes the loop count downward.
The + joins the text "Lap " with the current number, so each pass prints a different line: Lap 3, Lap 2, Lap 1.
This line sits outside the loop body, so it runs only once, after the counter drops below 1 and the loop ends.

prompts.prompt: Write an intro for loop to print a status list of 'Starting', 'Processing', 'Finished'.

explanation.summary: This program stores three status messages in an array and uses a counted for loop to print each one in order. It shows the standard Java pattern for walking through an array from the first element to the last.

lines.text: An array holds several values of the same type under one name, and the braces let you list the contents up front. The three strings live at positions 0, 1, and 2.

A for loop packs three parts into one line: start the counter at 0, keep going while i is less than the array's length, and add 1 to i after each pass. Using statuses.length instead of the number 3 means the loop still works if you add another status later.

Square brackets read the element at position i, so each pass prints the next status. Because counting starts at 0, the last valid index is length - 1, which is exactly where the condition above stops.

explanation.summary: This program stores three status messages in an array and prints each one using a for-each loop, which walks through every element without needing an index counter.

lines.text: An array holds a fixed sequence of values of the same type, and this initializer syntax creates the array and fills it with three strings in one step.
The for-each loop runs its body once per element of the array, assigning each element in turn to the variable status. Read the colon as "in": for each status in statuses.
Inside the loop, status already holds the current element, so there is no index arithmetic to get wrong.

examples.title: Pizza Order
examples.description: Write a simple program in Java for ordering pizza with 3 kinds of pizza options.
examples.prompt: Write an intro Java pizza order program that offers 3 kinds of pizza, a user chooses which pizza, and the order is displayed back.

explanation.summary: This program prints a numbered menu of three pizzas, reads the number the user types, and confirms the matching order (or reports an invalid choice). It combines an array, a for loop, and an if/else check on one small task.

lines.text: An array holds the three menu items in one named place, so the menu can be printed and looked up without repeating the names.
The loop counts from 0 up to one less than the array's length, which is exactly the range of valid array positions.
Arrays start at position 0, but people count from 1, so the displayed number is the index plus one.
Using print instead of println leaves the cursor on the same line, so the user types their answer next to the prompt.
A Scanner wrapped around System.in reads what the user types at the keyboard. Writing the full java.util.Scanner name avoids needing an import line.
hasNextInt checks that the next thing typed really is a whole number before reading it; if not, choice becomes -1, which will fail the range test below instead of crashing.
Both halves of the && must be true for the choice to be a real menu number, which guards against reading outside the array.
Subtracting one converts the user's 1-based menu number back into the matching array index.
Every input that is not a valid menu number lands here, so the program always tells the user what happened.
Closing the Scanner releases the input resource it was holding, a habit worth forming early.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Calling in the Functions
chapters.goal: Break down complicated programs into functions using static methods and learn about arguments, return types, and exception handling.

examples.title: Intro function example
examples.prompt: Could you write an intro function example?

explanation.summary: This program defines a small named block of code called a method (Java's word for a function) and runs it twice from main. It shows how naming a piece of work lets you reuse it without repeating the instructions.

lines.text: Every Java program lives inside a class, and the class name must match the file name, so this code belongs in IntroFunction.java.
This is the entry point: when you run the class, Java looks for exactly this method signature and starts here.
Calling the method by name runs the code in its body; the empty parentheses mean it needs no information passed in.
The same call a second time proves the real value of a method: one definition, as many uses as you like.
This defines the method. The word void says it hands nothing back to the caller, and static means it belongs to the class itself, so main can call it directly.
This is the single piece of work the method exists to do, which is why you see the message printed twice when the program runs.

examples.title: Java function access modifiers
examples.prompt: Could you create a relatable intro Java example that shows how the four function modifiers work? Please start from widest access to narrowest access in your examples.
response: // Widest access: anyone, anywhere can call this
System.out.println("Public: like posting on social media, anyone can see it.");
// Next: same package and subclasses (even in other packages)
System.out.println("Protected: like a family group chat, relatives (subclasses) and neighbors (same package) see it.");
// Next: package-private (no modifier) — only classes in the same package
System.out.println("Package-private: like a neighborhood bulletin, only locals (same package) see it.");
// Narrowest: only this class can use it
System.out.println("Private: like a personal diary, only you (this class) can read it.");

explanation.summary: This program demonstrates Java's four access levels for methods — public, protected, package-private, and private — by comparing each one to a way of sharing a message with people. All four are called from main inside the same class, which is the one place where every level is visible.

lines.text: The four sharing methods belong to an instance rather than the class itself, so main creates one object to call them on.
A public method can be called from any class in any package, so this call would work from anywhere.
A protected method is reachable here because main sits inside the same class; from outside, only the same package or a subclass could call it.
With no modifier at all, the method is package-private, so a class in a different package could not reach it.
A private method can only be called from within its own class, which is exactly where this call lives.
public is the widest access level, placing no restriction on who may call the method.
protected widens package-private access by also letting subclasses in other packages call the method.
Leaving the modifier off is a deliberate choice called package-private: the method is visible only to classes in the same package.
private is the narrowest level and is the default choice for helper methods you do not want other classes depending on.

examples.title: Java function return type code examples
examples.prompt: Write an intro Java program for basic houseplant care with functions using different return types and avoiding parameters.

explanation.summary: This program demonstrates the four kinds of return type a Java method can have: void (returns nothing), boolean, int, and String. Each method takes no parameters, so main simply calls them and prints whatever comes back.

lines.text: A void method is called as a statement on its own, because there is no value coming back to print or store.
The call to hasSunlight() is replaced by its returned value before printing, and the + joins that value onto the label text.
The keyword void declares that this method hands nothing back to the caller; it just does its work and finishes.
Declaring boolean promises the caller a true or false answer, which suits a yes-or-no question about sunlight.
The return statement sends the value back to whoever called the method and ends the method immediately.
